title: Family, community, participation
hook: in a garden with nothing yet gone wrong, God finds one thing that is not good

segments.voice: Yesterday, life and dignity: a crown on every head. Your line was every life. Did someone easy to overlook get your full attention? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

The garden is new. Nothing has gone wrong yet. No serpent, no fruit, no hiding. Again and again in Genesis, God looks at what he has made and sees that it is good. And then something isn't. Not danger. Not hunger. Solitude. In the Douay-Rheims: "It is not good for man to be alone." Catholic social teaching takes that sentence seriously. A person is made for other people, and a society is made of people taking part in it. Today, family, community, and participation, beginning with family.
screen: `A GARDEN WITH NOTHING WRONG.` → `ONE THING IS NOT GOOD.` → `ALONE.`

segments.voice: First, the claim underneath. The Catechism says the human person needs to live in society. It isn't an extra added later; it's part of how people are made. Catholics see a reflection of God in this too: they believe in one God who is three persons, a communion, so being made in God's image means being made for communion. Second, the family. The Catechism calls the family the original cell of social life. It's where a person first learns to be loved, to share, to forgive, to wait their turn at the table. So the teaching asks a society to protect and support families, and it says that when families are squeezed, the whole society feels it. Third, the wider circles. Between the family and the state there are many others: a parish, a union, a neighborhood, a team, a club. The Catechism says these voluntary associations should be encouraged, because they let people act together on what they share. The first Christians in Acts are described as persevering in fellowship; the Greek word is koinonia, sharing in common. Fourth, participation. The Catechism says it is necessary that all take part, each according to their position and role, in promoting the common good, and it calls this an obligation rooted in human dignity. Then it says where participation begins: not with running for office, but with what's already in your hands, caring for your family and doing your work well. And it asks that no one be shut out. A place where some people never get a voice isn't whole.
screen: `MADE FOR OTHERS.` · `THE FAMILY: THE ORIGINAL CELL.` · `WIDER CIRCLES OF COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `EVERYONE TAKES PART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one community effort to join. Settle, and breathe. Let the circles you belong to come into view, one at a time. Your household. Your street or building. Your parish, if you have one. Your workplace, your school, your team. Somewhere in those circles, something shared needs hands: a meal, a cleanup, a meeting nobody wants to go to, a sign-up sheet with empty lines. Pick one. Not to save it. Just to take part. If you pray, you can ask God to show you where. The bell holds the time.
Family. In Catholic social teaching, the original cell of social life, and the first circle in which everyone is meant to take part. Today's word.
Your line: everyone takes part. Today, take one small part in something shared: sign up, show up, or speak up once. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Catholics live this through family life, parish ministries and volunteer groups, and through unions, civic groups and local councils; some parishes invite members to join a ministry or serve on a parish council.

original.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing in common. the word for the first Christians' life together in Acts.

what a scholar hears: the Catechism's link between the communion of the three divine persons and the communion people are made for.

CCC 1913 paraphrased closely ('it is necessary that all participate, each according to his position and role, in promoting the common good'); not presented as a quotation because the English Catechism text is under copyright.
